design_detail: Randomized five-condition crossover pharmacokinetic study in 9 healthy non-smoking men in Linköping, Sweden. Each man received the same ethanol dose (0.30 g per kg body weight) on five occasions at least 7 days apart: drunk a few minutes after a breakfast rich in fat, in carbohydrate or in protein (about 3000 kJ each, eaten in 15 min), drunk after a 10-hour overnight fast, or infused intravenously over 30 min. Venous blood ethanol was measured by headspace gas chromatography for 210 min (sometimes 300 min). Outcomes: peak blood alcohol concentration (BAC), time to peak, and area under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 210 min (AUC); elimination rate, back-extrapolated intercept and volume of distribution for the fasting and intravenous conditions only. How the order was randomized is not described.
can_establish: Whether, in a few healthy young men given one small fixed amount of ethanol in the laboratory, a breakfast eaten just before drinking lowers the peak and the area of the blood alcohol curve compared with drinking on an empty stomach and with intravenous delivery, and by roughly how much.
cannot_establish: Whether the composition of the meal matters (the meal comparison had post hoc power of 0.22 to 0.25); what happens with larger amounts, in women, after other meals or other intervals between eating and drinking, or in everyday drinking; whether a lower BAC means less impairment (no effect measure); or by what mechanism (first-pass metabolism was inferred, not measured).

sample.recruitment: Paid volunteers; how they were recruited is not reported (Methods › Subjects and conditions, 1st paragraph, pp. 521–522). Hospital departments of forensic toxicology, clinical pharmacology and internal medicine in Linköping, Sweden.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy men, all non-smokers (p. 521). No other criteria are stated: usual drinking, medicines, health screening and liver tests are not reported.
sample.demographics: Mean age 24.6 years (SD 4.8), body weight 75.8 kg (SD 9.0), height 183 cm (SD 4.6) (pp. 521–522). No women.
sample.attrition: None reported; Table 1 gives n = 9 for every condition (p. 524).
sample.selection_effects: Nine young, healthy, non-smoking paid male volunteers whose drinking histories are not described. The results cannot be assumed to hold for women, older people, people who drink heavily, people with liver disease or people taking medicines.

exposure.measurement: Ethanol was given by the investigators: ethanol diluted with orange juice to 20% v/v and finished within exactly 15 min, or a 6% w/v solution in saline infused at a constant rate over 30 min by pump (Methods › Subjects and conditions, 1st paragraph, p. 522). Breakfasts of ordinary Swedish foods chosen with a dietician were eaten in 15 min and the drink was taken a few minutes later (2nd paragraph, p. 522; acknowledgement, p. 525).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one dose of 0.30 g ethanol per kg body weight in every session. Fat-rich meal 2908 kJ (fat 55%, carbohydrate 33%, protein 12% of energy); carbohydrate-rich meal 2924 kJ (9%, 86%, 6%); protein-rich meal 3188 kJ (24%, 45%, 31%); fasting condition after a 10-hour overnight fast; intravenous infusion over 30 min on an empty stomach (p. 522; Table 1, p. 524). Sessions at least 7 days apart, intervals differing between participants (p. 522).
exposure.polysubstance: All participants were non-smokers; other drug use, usual alcohol intake and medicines are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Overnight fast of 10 hours before the fasting and intravenous sessions (p. 522); whether alcohol was avoided before sessions is not reported.

comparison.controls: Within-person: every man completed all five conditions, so the overnight-fast and intravenous sessions are the reference conditions for the three meal conditions.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person design). The meals were meant to be of similar energy, but the protein-rich meal provided about 9 to 10% more energy than the other two (editors' calculation from Table 1, p. 524).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Usual drinking, liver function, gastric emptying and the activity or genotype of alcohol-metabolizing enzymes were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (within-person comparison); other drug use not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Venous blood through an indwelling catheter before dosing and at 10, 20, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180 and 210 min, sometimes to 300 min; ethanol by headspace gas chromatography with n-propanol as internal standard, limit of quantification 1 mg/dl, SD 0.8 mg/dl (coefficient of variation under 1%) at 100 mg/dl, accuracy checked against purchased known-strength standards of 50, 100 and 150 mg/dl (Methods › Sampling of blood, p. 522). Peak BAC and time to peak read from the data; AUC by the linear trapezoidal rule from 0 to 210 min; for the fasting and intravenous conditions only, the zero-order disappearance rate (ko), the back-extrapolated intercept (Co) and the apparent volume of distribution (Vd) (Methods › Pharmacokinetics of ethanol, p. 522).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard pharmacokinetic quantities and a forensic analytical method. The authors state that bioavailability cannot be computed as an AUC ratio because ethanol elimination is saturable, so AUC is used only to compare conditions given the same dose (p. 522).
outcomes.operationalization: Systemic availability of ethanol was represented by peak BAC and AUC in each meal condition compared with the fasting and intravenous conditions. No measure of impairment, subjective effect or harm.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Seven tests: two five-condition ANOVAs (peak BAC, AUC), two ANOVAs across the three meals, and three fasting-versus-intravenous comparisons (ko, Co, Vd). The shorter elimination time in the fed state was not tested.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported and not possible for participants (meal, fast or infusion obvious); the outcome is an objective laboratory measure.

analysis.effect_sizes: Mean (SD), n = 9 (Table 1, p. 524). Peak BAC, mg/dl: fat-rich 16.6 (4.0), carbohydrate-rich 17.7 (7.1), protein-rich 13.3 (4.0), fasting 30.8 (4.3), intravenous 54.3 (6.4). AUC 0–210 min, mg/dl·min: 1767 (549), 1619 (760), 1270 (406), 3210 (527) and 4786 (446). Five conditions: F = 98.7 (peak) and 88.9 (AUC), df 4 and 32, P < 0.001; three meals: F = 2.22 and 2.42, P > 0.05 (pp. 523–524). Editors' calculation: the meal peaks were 43% to 57% of the fasting peak and the meal AUCs 40% to 55% of the fasting AUC; the fasting peak and AUC were 57% and 67% of the intravenous values. No meal-versus-fasting test is printed; using the five-condition residual SD (5.1 mg/dl; 465.2 mg/dl·min), each meal-fasting difference is about 5 to 9 times its approximate standard error (editors' calculation, assumes sphericity). Between meals, the protein-rich meal gave a peak about 20% and 25% lower than the fat-rich and carbohydrate-rich meals, and an AUC about 28% and 22% lower (editors' calculation), not significant. Fasting versus intravenous: ko 10.3 (1.8) versus 9.8 (1.2) mg/dl per hour, 95% CI of the difference −2.27 to 1.25; Co 37 (4.9) versus 40 (3.9) mg/dl, CI −1.6 to 7.0; Vd 0.81 (0.11) versus 0.75 (0.08) l/kg, CI −0.154 to 0.033 (p. 523).
analysis.covariates: None; one-way repeated-measures ANOVA and paired t-tests (SigmaStat) (p. 522).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (1997). The protocol was approved by the local ethics committee (p. 522).
analysis.selective_reporting: The Methods say paired t-tests were used when two treatments were compared, but no meal-versus-fasting test is reported; the only test including the fasting condition is the five-condition ANOVA, whose result is driven partly by the intravenous condition. The shorter elimination time in the fed state is stated as 1 to 2 hours without measured values. No elimination rate could be fitted for the meal conditions (p. 522).
analysis.power: No calculation in advance. Post hoc power was 1.0 for the five-condition ANOVAs and 0.22 (peak) and 0.25 (AUC) for the three-meal comparison, which the authors say calls for caution (p. 523; Table 1 footnotes, p. 524).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 9 healthy young men given 0.30 g ethanol per kg, drinking a few minutes after a breakfast of about 3000 kJ roughly halved the peak BAC (13 to 18 mg/dl against 31 mg/dl after an overnight fast) and the AUC over 210 min (1270 to 1767 against 3210 mg/dl·min), with larger differences between people after food (coefficients of variation 24% to 47%). The three meals did not differ significantly, but the protein-rich meal gave the lowest values and the comparison had power of about 0.2. Even on an empty stomach, peak and AUC were lower than with intravenous infusion of the same dose (57% and 67%). The fed-state curves could not be fitted, so no fed-state elimination rate was estimated.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that drinking after a meal, regardless of its composition, decreases the systemic availability of ethanol, and explains this by hepatic first-pass metabolism (p. 521); the final paragraph calls composition not so important (p. 525). Gaps: (1) the composition statement rests on a non-significant comparison that the authors themselves say had low power (p. 523), and differences of 20% to 28% between meals were seen but could not be tested reliably; (2) first-pass metabolism and the alternative two-pool absorption mechanism were not measured; the authors offer both (pp. 524–525); (3) the statement that elimination took 1 to 2 hours less in the fed state (abstract, p. 521; Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 523) and that disposal was boosted is not quantified; a lower curve reaches zero sooner even at an unchanged elimination rate, and the fasting curves were still above zero when sampling ended (Figure 1, p. 523); (4) a more pronounced effect when the meal is closer to drinking is cited as unpublished work (p. 525). The central result, lower peak and AUC after food at this small dose, is reported accurately.

timeline.event: Welling (1977) and Wilkinson et al. (1977): earlier fasted and fed studies of small ethanol doses, cited by the paper as showing a lower peak and BAC profile after food (refs 7 and 11); not read.

Rogers et al. (1987): cited as finding carbohydrate-rich food more effective than fat or protein in accelerating ethanol metabolism, by an unexplained mechanism (ref 28); not read. This conflicts with the present null comparison of meals.
Jones and Jönsson (1994): the same group's earlier study of food-induced lowering of peak BAC and faster elimination immediately after a meal (ref 10); not read.
Fraser et al. (1995): variability of ethanol profiles with ingestion before or after an evening meal (ref 6); not read.
This study: five-condition crossover in 9 men at 0.30 g/kg.
Ramchandani et al. (2001): food and food composition and alcohol elimination rates in healthy men and women, listed as a further study on the BeforeDuring reading list; not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The lowering of peak BAC and AUC by food before drinking agrees with the earlier fed-versus-fasting studies the paper cites, none of which was read for this card. Whether macronutrient composition matters is unsettled: this study was underpowered for it and a cited study found a carbohydrate effect on metabolism. The evidence is from small laboratory studies at small doses; the BeforeDuring list records that no naturalistic study of food before drinking was found.

funding.funder: Supported in part by grants from the Swedish National Board of Forensic Medicine and the Forensic Science Centre, Linköping (acknowledgement, p. 525).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: First author from the Department of Forensic Toxicology, National Laboratory of Forensic Chemistry, Linköping; co-authors from clinical pharmacology and internal medicine. The paper frames its question around estimating BAC in medicolegal casework (pp. 521, 525). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized crossover study in women and men, at several doses including amounts typical of a drinking occasion, with meals that differ in composition at matched energy and volume and at several intervals before drinking, blood sampled until BAC reaches zero, and measures of impairment as well as BAC.

domains.note: A randomized crossover order is stated (abstract; Methods, p. 522), but how the order was generated and concealed, and which order each man received, are not reported; with five conditions and nine men the orders cannot have been balanced.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: At least 7 days between sessions after a single small dose eliminated within hours (Figure 1), so carryover is implausible; period was not in the analysis and intervals varied between men.
Supervised laboratory sessions with fixed meals, timed drinking and pump infusion; no deviations reported. Open conditions, but the outcome does not depend on expectations.
All 9 men contribute to every condition in Table 1 (p. 524). The printed degrees of freedom for the three-meal ANOVA (2 and 17) do not match complete data from 9 men (2 and 16); see reporting issues.

Blood ethanol by a validated headspace gas chromatography method with stated precision (p. 522). AUC stops at 210 min while fasting and intravenous concentrations were still above zero, which if anything understates the fed-fasting difference.

No protocol; the meal-versus-fasting comparisons that the Methods imply (paired t-tests) are not reported; the fed-state elimination time is asserted without values; the sampling times visible in Figure 1 do not match the stated schedule.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The outcome is objective, the design is within-person and the fed-fasting difference is large relative to its variability, so bias is unlikely to explain it; concerns come from an undescribed randomization and incomplete reporting of the planned comparisons. The main limits are precision and directness rather than bias: 9 young men, one small dose, breakfasts eaten just before drinking. Citable for: lower peak BAC and AUC after a meal than on an empty stomach at 0.30 g/kg in healthy men, with values (Table 1). Not citable for: meal composition having no effect, the mechanism, the size of the effect at larger doses or in women, or any effect on impairment.

key_findings.finding: Nine healthy non-smoking men (mean age 24.6 years, SD 4.8; weight 75.8 kg, SD 9.0) each received ethanol 0.30 g/kg in five sessions at least 7 days apart, in randomized order: after a fat-rich, a carbohydrate-rich or a protein-rich breakfast, after a 10-hour overnight fast, or by intravenous infusion over 30 min.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods; Methods › Subjects and conditions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The breakfasts provided 2908 kJ (fat-rich: 55% of energy from fat), 2924 kJ (carbohydrate-rich: 86% from carbohydrate) and 3188 kJ (protein-rich: 31% from protein, 45% from carbohydrate); each was eaten in 15 min and the drink was finished within 15 min a few minutes later.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Subjects and conditions, 2nd paragraph (p. 522); Table 1 (p. 524)

key_findings.finding: Peak BAC, mean (SD), mg/dl: 16.6 (4.0) after the fat-rich meal, 17.7 (7.1) after the carbohydrate-rich meal, 13.3 (4.0) after the protein-rich meal, 30.8 (4.3) after an overnight fast and 54.3 (6.4) with intravenous infusion.
AUC from 0 to 210 min, mean (SD), mg/dl·min: 1767 (549) fat-rich, 1619 (760) carbohydrate-rich, 1270 (406) protein-rich, 3210 (527) fasting and 4786 (446) intravenous.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: meal peaks 43% to 57% of the fasting peak, meal AUCs 40% to 55% of the fasting AUC.

key_findings.finding: Across all five conditions the differences were significant (F = 98.7 for peak BAC and 88.9 for AUC, df 4 and 32, P < 0.001, post hoc power 1.0); no test of each meal against fasting is reported.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (starts p. 522, F values on p. 523); Table 1 and footnote 3 (p. 524)

key_findings.finding: The three meals did not differ significantly (F = 2.22 for peak BAC and 2.42 for AUC, P > 0.05); post hoc power was 0.22 and 0.25, and the authors say the result should be read with caution.
key_findings.note: The protein-rich meal gave the lowest peak and AUC; the authors call this a non-significant tendency (Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 524).

key_findings.finding: Time to peak ranged from 30 to 90 min after the fat-rich and carbohydrate-rich meals, 30 to 60 min after the protein-rich meal and on an empty stomach, and was 30 min (end of infusion) intravenously.
Variability between people was greatest after food: coefficients of variation 24% to 40% for peak BAC and 31% to 47% for AUC after the meals, against 14% and 16% fasting and 12% and 10% intravenous.

Fasting and intravenous conditions did not differ in disappearance rate (10.3, SD 1.8, versus 9.8, SD 1.2 mg/dl per hour; 95% CI of the difference −2.27 to 1.25), intercept (37 versus 40 mg/dl; CI −1.6 to 7.0) or volume of distribution (0.81 versus 0.75 l/kg; CI −0.154 to 0.033).

After food, individual peaks were often below 10 to 15 mg/dl and some curves showed a secondary peak hours after drinking, so curves could not be fitted and no elimination rate was estimated for the meal conditions.

The statement that elimination from blood took 1 to 2 hours less in the fed state comes from inspection of Figure 1, not from a measured or tested quantity. Editors' reading of the mean curves (Figure 1f): the meal curves reach about zero at roughly 190 to 200 min; the fasting curve's last plotted point is at about 190 min, with a dashed extension reaching zero at roughly 235 min; the intravenous curve is still about 1 mg/dl at 300 min.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 521); Discussion, 1st paragraph and Figure 1 (p. 523)
key_findings.note: Values read from a 600-dpi crop of Figure 1f and approximate. On this reading the fed-fasting difference in time to zero is under an hour and partly extrapolated.

key_findings.finding: The authors explain the lower BAC after food by slow, variable gastric emptying allowing hepatic first-pass metabolism under Michaelis-Menten kinetics, or by a two-pool model in which part of the dose is bound to the meal; neither was measured in this study.

The disappearance rate in the fasting and intravenous conditions (about 10 mg/dl per hour) was lower than the 15 mg/dl per hour the authors say is often cited for moderate drinkers; they attribute this to the 10 to 12 hour fast, citing earlier work.

reporting_issues.issue: The three-meal ANOVA is printed with 2 and 17 degrees of freedom; with 9 men measured under 3 conditions a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA has 2 and 16 (the five-condition ANOVA's 4 and 32 is correct).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the p-values are about 0.14 (peak) and 0.12 (AUC) with either df (editors' calculation), so the conclusion is unchanged, but a value may be missing or the df mistyped.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list blood samples at 10, 20, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180 and 210 min (sometimes 300 min), but in the editors' reading of Figure 1 the individual curves in panels a–d end at about 190 min and the mean curves in Figure 1f show points at roughly 10-minute intervals from 150 min onwards (and from 210 to 300 min for the intravenous condition); AUC is said to run from 0 to 210 min.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sampling actually behind the AUC and the elimination-time statement cannot be reconstructed. Fasting and intravenous concentrations were still above zero at the end of the window, so their AUCs are truncated, which makes the reported fed-fasting contrast conservative rather than inflated.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes large inter- and intra-individual variation, but each condition was given once to each man, so variation within a person under the same condition was not measured.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only between-person variation (the coefficients of variation in Table 1) is supported by the data.

reporting_issues.issue: The meals are described as similar in volume and energy (abstract; Table 1 title), but meal volume or weight is not reported and the protein-rich meal provided 3188 kJ against 2908 and 2924 kJ, about 9 to 10% more (editors' calculation); it also took more of its energy from carbohydrate (45%) than from protein (31%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The meal with the lowest BAC was also the largest in energy, and the macronutrient contrast is weaker than the labels suggest; any composition effect, or its absence, is confounded with meal size.

reporting_issues.issue: The coefficient of variation for the intravenous AUC is printed as 10%, but by the editors' calculation 446/4786 is 9.3%; the other coefficients match their means and SDs.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial rounding or transcription error; no effect on interpretation.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Br J Clin Pharmacol 44: 521–526, pp. 521–526 (all pages, including acknowledgement and references; text extracted and every number checked on the pages rendered at 150 dpi; Table 1 checked on the rendered page; Figure 1 read at 300 and 600 dpi, values read from it labelled approximate; no supplement).
